new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's gordon record (final stress = fixed final). It is a second-hand summary in a grammar of a sister language, citing Clayre 1992 and Blust 1999 (Long Banga' Sa'ban), not a primary Sa'ban description.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sa'ban varieties have predominantly word-final stress (secondary statement: Mortensen cites Clayre 1992 and Blust 1999 rather than his own Sa'ban data); the strong final stress is given as the trigger of Sa'ban's dramatic left-edge erosion sound changes.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Sa'ban itself ('predominantly final'). Regional caveat on the same page, about Lun Bawang/Kelabit rather than Sa'ban: Blust (2006:315) is quoted that northern Sarawak languages commonly show 'final stress in citation forms but penultimate stress in phrasal context', which Mortensen says could also mean regular penultimate stress plus a boundary tone; and stress is reconstructed as penultimate at Proto-North-Sarawak depth.
new_statements.identity_note: Mortensen speaks of 'the Sa'ban varieties' collectively; the Sa'ban data he uses elsewhere are Long Banga' Sa'ban from Blust (1999), and he places Long Banga' as the westernmost Sa'ban dialect on the upper Baram (Sarawak). Clayre 1973's exact locale could not be checked since the article was not opened.

sources.quote: Merap and Sa'ban both shifted stress to the final syllable, where word-final stress wreaked havoc on the conservative phonologies of Proto-Kelabit as well as Proto-Ngorek-Merap.
sources.note: One-line area-comparison statement, not a description; Sa'ban material is cited from Blust (2001), not the author's own data. Also lists Kiput, Berawan, Modang, Gaai, Kelai and Hliboi Bidayuh as stress-final-shift languages of the area (conclusion p. 175).
